subject: Career
title: Confirmation Bias in Interviews
description: A 60-second lesson on Confirmation Bias in Interviews.

hook.text: An interviewer reads your resume and forms an opinion. The interview becomes a search for proof.

buildup.text: Confirmation bias: we seek information that supports what we already believe.

discovery.text: If they liked your resume, they'll hear your strengths. If not, they'll notice every flaw.

twist.text: Structured interviews reduce this — same questions, same order, scored on rubrics.

climax.text: As a candidate, your best defense is a strong opening. It sets the confirmation in your favor.

punchline.text: Bias is the default. Structure is the fix.

quiz.question: How does confirmation bias affect interviews?
options: Interviewers seek evidence supporting their initial impression
They forget everything after the interview
They always prefer the last candidate

details.summary: Confirmation bias leads interviewers to seek evidence that supports their initial impression while ignoring contradictory information. Once a hypothesis forms, questions unconsciously shift to confirm rather than challenge it.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding confirmation bias helps candidates steer the narrative early, because the interviewer's initial hypothesis becomes self-reinforcing throughout the conversation.
takeaways: Interviewers often decide within minutes then seek confirming evidence
Candidates should front-load their strongest credentials
Structured interviews with preset questions reduce confirmation bias

faq.question: How does confirmation bias differ from the halo effect in interviews?
faq.answer: The halo effect is about one trait coloring overall perception, while confirmation bias is about selectively seeking supporting evidence for an existing belief. They often work together, as a halo-triggered positive impression leads to confirmatory questioning.

faq.question: What can candidates do if they sense the interviewer has a negative initial impression?
faq.answer: Proactively introduce strong evidence that contradicts the negative hypothesis. Mentioning a relevant accomplishment or metric that directly addresses the likely concern can disrupt the confirmation loop before it solidifies.
